big_idea: Spoken words are made of separate sounds. We can ISOLATE and SEGMENT them.
learning_intention: We are learning to isolate and segment sounds in CVC words.
student_learning_goal: I can isolate and segment sounds in CVC words.
success_criteria: I can SAY the first sound of a word.
I can SAY the last sound of a word.
I can SEGMENT a CVC word into 3 sounds.
I can BLEND 3 sounds back into a word.
lesson_specific_materials: 3-Box Sound Box Cards (drawn with marker on index cards)
8 picture cards per pair (cut from any source)
3 counters per pair (bottle caps, paper clips, or any small classroom items)
OPTIONAL: a stuffed animal or sock as Sounder Sam

minds_on.hook: Sounder Sam: HOO HOO! Friends — every word is made of SOUNDS. Listen: /s/-/u/-/n/. SUN!
minds_on.teacher_script:
Bring children to the carpet. Hold up Sounder Sam (a stuffed animal, sock, or just gesture if no puppet). 'Reader friends — meet Sounder Sam! Sounder hears every SOUND in a word. Today we learn words are made of SOUNDS called PHONEMES.'

Define. 'A PHONEME is a SOUND in a spoken word. SUN has THREE sounds: /s/-/u/-/n/.'

Demo. Say SUN slowly, one finger per sound: '/s/ first, /u/ middle, /n/ last. Three phonemes, three fingers!'

Class echoes by clapping: /s/ clap, /u/ clap, /n/ clap. Together: '/s/-/u/-/n/. SUN!'

Repeat with MAT and CAT, three claps each.

'Sounder says — every CVC word has THREE sounds!'

FIRST-sound drill. Class shouts only the first sound.
BAG → '/b/!' PIN → '/p/!' RUG → '/r/!' TOP → '/t/!'

LAST-sound drill. Class shouts only the last sound.
BAG → /g/. PIN → /n/. RUG → /g/. TOP → /p/.

Segment drill. Class breaks a word into 3 sounds.
DOG → '/d/-/o/-/g/!' HAT → '/h/-/a/-/t/!'

'Sounder says — when you BREAK a word into sounds, you SEGMENT! New word: SEGMENT.'

Close with the refrain. 'HOO knows the sounds? YOU do!' Class chants it back.

steps.instruction: Hand each pair a Sound Box Card, 3 counters, and 8 picture cards.
Pairs take turns: name the picture, clap the sounds, push one counter into each box as they say each sound.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say: 'Push a counter for each sound.'

steps.instruction: After all 3 counters are placed, partner says the whole word back.
Stretch: pairs identify ONLY the first sound of 4 more pictures.

steps.teacher_prompt: Stop at each pair. Listen for accurate phonemes.

differentiation.for_emerging: Use 4 pictures only; teacher segments first as a model.
differentiation.for_extending: Ask the child to substitute the first sound (CAT → MAT).
differentiation.for_ell_or_iep: Picture cards with familiar items only; gesture each sound.
differentiation.for_movement_learners: Use whole-body sound: jump for first, hop for middle, stomp for last.

formative_check.what_to_look_for: Five signals: names picture; isolates first sound; isolates last sound; segments into three; blends back.

consolidation.exit_routine: Each child segments ONE word: 'I heard /__/-/__/-/__/, that's ___.' Class chants 'HOO knows the sounds? YOU do!'

assessment_in_this_lesson.evidence_collected: Tracker of phoneme isolation and segmentation.
assessment_in_this_lesson.rationale: Lesson 1 sets the baseline for phonemic awareness.

expanded_walkthrough.title: When the child says LETTER NAMES instead of SOUNDS — repairing the letter-name interference trap at Grade 1
expanded_walkthrough.rationale: The most common Grade-1 trap on B2.1: child segments CAT as 'cee-ay-tee' (letter NAMES) instead of '/c/-/a/-/t/' (sounds). This is canonical letter-name interference, Ehri's Phase 2 (2005). It signals the child has letter knowledge but hasn't linked names to phonological output yet.
expanded_walkthrough.setup: Segment activity. Child names CAT picture and says 'cee-ay-tee' instead of '/c/-/a/-/t/'.
expanded_walkthrough.teacher_script:
Crouch beside the child. 'Sounder asks — those are LETTER NAMES. We need SOUNDS.'

Probe. 'Listen carefully to me. /c/ (short cuh sound, no -ee). /a/ (short ah). /t/ (tuh, no -ee). Try with me: /c/-/a/-/t/.'

Generalise. 'Sounder says — letters have NAMES (cee, ay, tee) and SOUNDS (/c/, /a/, /t/). When we segment, we listen for the SOUNDS.'

If the child still uses names: contrast directly. 'The NAME is cee. The SOUND is /c/. The NAME is tee. The SOUND is /t/. Different!'

If still confused: use a known mismatch. 'The letter W — its NAME is doubleyou. But its SOUND is /w/. The name is not the sound!'
expected_student_responses: (Stretched) Says 'name is cee, sound is /c/' on their own
common_misconceptions: Letter names = sounds. (Repair: contrast each one.)
Long letter names like 'ay' have an extra sound. (Repair: short, clean phoneme.)
recovery_moves: Cover the picture and ask only for sounds (no name cue).
Contrast the name and sound side by side: 'cee... /c/'.
Use the doubleyou/W demonstration to show name and sound differ.
Practice with 3 known-easy CVC words before re-attempting.

worksheet_brief.purpose: Independent practice of phoneme isolation and segmentation.

parts_outline.task: First-sound match: 4 picture cards with 4 phoneme bubbles. Draw a line from each picture to its starting sound.
Sound boxes: 4 pictures with a 3-cell sound box below each. Write or mark one phoneme per box.
Last-sound circle: 3 pictures with 3 phoneme choices each. Circle the LAST sound. Two pictures are NEW words to check transfer.
